title: Garbage Collection & Memory Management
tagline: Who frees your memory, when, and at what cost — from malloc and reference counting to V8, the JVM, Go, and Rust's ownership model.

sections.content:
Every object your program creates occupies memory, and memory is finite. At some point that memory must be given back so it can be reused. **Memory management** is the question of *who* decides when an object is no longer needed, and *how* its space is reclaimed. Get it wrong in one direction and you **leak**: memory grows until the process slows down or is killed. Get it wrong in the other and you free something still in use — a **use-after-free** that corrupts data, crashes, or opens a security hole.

There are three broad answers. In **manual** memory management (C, C++ without smart pointers), the programmer calls `free` or `delete`. In **automatic** memory management, a **garbage collector (GC)** in the runtime finds objects the program can no longer reach and reclaims them — JavaScript, Java, C#, Go, Python, and most modern languages work this way. And in **ownership-based** management (Rust, and C++ RAII), the compiler inserts the frees at statically known points, giving deterministic cleanup with no runtime collector.

Garbage collection removes an entire class of bugs, but it is not free and not magic. Collectors spend CPU time, sometimes pause your program, need extra memory headroom, and cannot save you from the most common kind of leak in managed languages: objects that are *still reachable* but that you will never use again — a forgotten listener, an unbounded cache, a closure holding a huge array.

This chapter covers manual vs automatic management, reachability and GC roots, reference counting and its cycle problem (and how CPython and Swift deal with it), the three tracing algorithms (mark-sweep, mark-compact, copying), the generational hypothesis, stop-the-world vs incremental and concurrent collection, tri-color marking and write barriers, how V8, the JVM, and Go actually collect, Rust's ownership alternative, weak references and finalizers, and how to hunt real JavaScript leaks with heap snapshots. It builds on the Stack & Heap chapter.

sections.title: Cleaning a Shared Office
sections.content:
Imagine an open-plan office where people leave documents on desks.

**Manual management** is "everyone shreds their own documents". Efficient and predictable — but someone always forgets (a leak), and occasionally someone shreds a document a colleague is still reading (use-after-free).

**Reference counting** is a sticky note on each document listing how many people are using it. Each person who takes a copy adds a tick; each who finishes removes one. When the count hits zero, the document is shredded immediately. Simple — until two documents reference each other ("see appendix B" / "see main report A"). Nobody is reading either, but each keeps the other's count at one, so neither is ever shredded.

**Tracing garbage collection** is the night cleaner. They do not trust the sticky notes; they start from things that are definitely in use — documents on the desks of people currently in the building (the **roots**) — and follow every "see also" reference, marking each document they reach. Anything not marked by the end of the walk is shredded, cycles included. The cost is that the cleaner needs time, and if they insist the whole office stops working while they walk around (**stop-the-world**), everyone notices.

A **generational** cleaner notices that most documents are scratch notes thrown away within minutes, so they sweep the "inbox tray" very often and the archive cabinets rarely. A **concurrent** cleaner works while people are still at their desks, but then needs a rule — "if you put a new document into a folder I already checked, flag it for me" — which is exactly what a **write barrier** is.

sections.title: Manual vs Automatic Memory Management
sections.content:
In **manual** memory management, the programmer requests heap memory (`malloc`, `new`) and must explicitly release it (`free`, `delete`). It gives full control and predictable performance — no collector pauses, no extra headroom — which is why kernels, embedded systems, game engines, and databases are still written this way. But the error modes are severe:

- **Memory leak** — forgetting to free. Memory grows until exhaustion.
- **Use-after-free / dangling pointer** — using memory after freeing it; the space may already hold another object.
- **Double free** — freeing twice, corrupting the allocator's bookkeeping.
- **Buffer overflow** — writing past an allocation's end (not strictly a lifetime bug, but the same unsafety).

These are not just crashes: Microsoft (2019) and the Chromium project (2020) each reported that roughly **70% of their serious security vulnerabilities were memory-safety bugs**, which is why governments and industry now push memory-safe languages for new code.

C++ mitigates manual management with **RAII** (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization): a destructor runs automatically when an object goes out of scope, so `std::unique_ptr` frees its pointee deterministically and `std::shared_ptr` adds reference counting. That handles most cases but cannot prevent every dangling reference.

**Automatic** memory management hands the job to the runtime. The two families are **reference counting** (free an object when its count of incoming references reaches zero) and **tracing GC** (periodically find everything reachable and reclaim the rest). Most production runtimes use tracing — V8, JVM, .NET, Go — while CPython, Swift, and Objective-C are built on reference counting.

The trade-offs of automatic management, in one list: **CPU overhead** (often a few percent to tens of percent of runtime, depending on allocation rate and tuning), **pauses** (from milliseconds down to sub-millisecond in modern concurrent collectors), **memory headroom** (tracing collectors typically perform well only when the heap is noticeably larger than the live data — frequently cited as 2x or more), and **non-deterministic timing** of reclamation, which is why you must never rely on GC to close files or sockets.

sections.title: Reachability and GC Roots
sections.content:
A collector cannot know which objects you *will* use in the future, so every real GC uses a conservative stand-in: an object is **live** if it is **reachable** — if some chain of references leads to it from a **root**. Everything unreachable is garbage, because the program has no way to ever touch it again.

**Roots** are references the program can use directly without going through another heap object:

- **Local variables and temporaries** in every active stack frame (and CPU registers) of every thread.
- **Global variables** — in JavaScript, properties of `globalThis` and module-level bindings of loaded modules.
- **Runtime-internal references** — the job and task queues (pending promise reactions, scheduled timers), active event listeners registered with the browser or Node, handles held by native code, compiled code that embeds object constants.

From the roots, the object graph is followed transitively. Note what this implies:

1. **Reachable is not the same as useful.** An entry in a global `Map` you will never read again is reachable, so it is never collected. This is the root cause of essentially every leak in GC'd languages.
2. **Cycles are fine for tracing collectors.** Two objects referencing each other but unreachable from any root are garbage like anything else.
3. **A single root can retain a huge subgraph.** One forgotten listener on `window` can keep alive its closure, which holds a component, which holds a detached DOM tree with thousands of nodes. In a heap snapshot this appears as a large **retained size** — the memory that would be freed if that object were collected.

Some collectors are **precise** (they know exactly which words are pointers — V8, the JVM, Go) and some are **conservative** (they treat any word that *looks like* a pointer as one, as the Boehm collector for C does). Conservative scanning can keep garbage alive by accident but works without compiler cooperation.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  R1["Root: stack frame of main"] --> A["app object"]
  R2["Root: globalThis"] --> L["listener registry"]
  A --> B["user session"]
  B --> C["profile"]
  L --> H["handler closure"]
  H --> T["big table - still reachable"]
  X["parent node"] --> Y["child node"]
  Y --> X
  Z["old buffer"]
sections.caption: Reachability from the roots. app, session, profile, and the listener chain are live; the big table stays alive only because a forgotten handler references it. The parent and child cycle and the old buffer are unreachable, so a tracing collector reclaims them.

sections.title: Reference Counting: Immediate, Simple, and Blind to Cycles
sections.content:
**Reference counting (RC)** stores a counter in each object: the number of references pointing at it. Creating a reference increments it; dropping one decrements it; when the count reaches **zero**, the object is freed immediately and the counts of everything it pointed to are decremented in turn (possibly cascading).

Strengths:

- **Prompt, deterministic reclamation.** Memory is returned the moment the last reference disappears, so peak memory stays low and destructors run at predictable times (CPython closes a file when its last reference dies — although you should still use `with`).
- **No global pauses** for tracing, and work is spread evenly across the program.
- **Simple to implement** and easy to integrate with native code.

Weaknesses:

- **Cycles leak.** A parent that references its child and a child that references its parent keep each other's counts at 1 forever, even when nothing else can reach them. Doubly linked lists, trees with parent pointers, observer pairs, and closures that capture themselves all create cycles.
- **Overhead on every pointer write.** Each assignment updates two counters; in multithreaded code those updates must be **atomic**, which is expensive. Cache traffic increases because even reading-only code touches counts.
- **Cascading frees** can still cause pauses: dropping the root of a million-node tree frees a million objects right there.

How real systems handle cycles:

- **CPython** uses reference counting as its primary mechanism and adds a **cycle collector** (the `gc` module) that periodically looks for groups of container objects referenced only by each other. It is generational: young container objects are examined most often. The free-threaded build (PEP 703, officially supported since Python 3.14) switches to **biased reference counting** to make counts cheap without the GIL.
- **Swift and Objective-C** use **ARC** (Automatic Reference Counting): the *compiler* inserts retain/release calls. There is **no cycle collector**, so programmers break cycles explicitly with `weak` references (which become `nil` when the target is freed) or `unowned` references. The classic iOS leak is a closure stored on `self` that captures `self` strongly; the fix is `[weak self]`.
- **C++ `shared_ptr`/`weak_ptr`** and **Rust `Rc`/`Arc`/`Weak`** are library-level reference counting with the same rule: back-pointers must be weak.

Early JavaScript engines (old Internet Explorer's DOM/COM objects) were reference counted, which made DOM ↔ JavaScript cycles leak. All modern JS engines use tracing collectors, so cycles are not a leak source in JavaScript today.

sections.label: Reference counting vs tracing
sections.explanation: The toy heap tracks a count per object. Dropping `cache` takes its count to zero and RC frees it instantly. Dropping `parent` only lowers its count from 2 to 1, because `child` still points back at it — so the unreachable cycle survives reference counting. `markSweep()` ignores counts, walks from the root `app`, never reaches the cycle, and sweeps both objects. This is the same division of labour as CPython: refcounting for the common case, a tracing cycle collector for the rest.

sections.title: Tracing GC: Mark-Sweep, Mark-Compact, and Copying
sections.content:
A **tracing collector** finds live objects by traversing the graph from the roots, then reclaims everything else. All tracing collectors share a **mark** (or trace) phase and differ in what they do with the result.

**Mark-sweep** (John McCarthy, Lisp, 1960). Mark every reachable object (usually a bit in the header or a side bitmap), then **sweep** the heap linearly, adding unmarked blocks to **free lists** for reuse. Objects never move, which is simple and plays well with native code holding raw pointers. The downside is **fragmentation**: free space ends up as many small holes, so a large allocation can fail even when total free memory is plentiful, and allocation needs a free-list search. Sweeping cost is proportional to the *heap size*.

**Mark-compact.** Mark, then **slide** all live objects together to one end of the region and update every pointer to them. Fragmentation disappears and allocation becomes a **bump pointer** (just increment an address — as fast as stack allocation). The cost is extra passes over the heap and the need to fix up every reference, so it is the most expensive per collection. Collectors often compact selectively — only regions that are badly fragmented.

**Copying / semispace** (Cheney's algorithm, 1970). Split the space in two halves: allocate in *from-space*; when it fills, copy every reachable object into *to-space* (compacting them as a side effect), leave forwarding addresses behind, then swap roles. Cost is proportional to the **live data only** — dead objects are never even touched — which makes it ideal when most objects are dead. The catch: half the space is always idle, and copying long-lived large objects repeatedly is wasteful.

| | Moves objects | Fragmentation | Cost proportional to | Space overhead |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mark-sweep | No | Yes | Heap size (sweep) | Low |
| Mark-compact | Yes | No | Heap size, multiple passes | Low |
| Copying | Yes | No | Live objects only | 2x for the copied region |

Real collectors combine them: copy the young generation where almost everything is dead, mark-sweep the old generation most of the time, and compact the fragmented parts occasionally.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  S["GC triggered"] --> M["Mark: trace from roots, flag live objects"]
  M --> Q{"What to do with dead space?"}
  Q -->|"mark-sweep"| SW["Sweep: dead blocks to free lists"]
  Q -->|"mark-compact"| CO["Slide live objects together, fix pointers"]
  Q -->|"copying"| CP["Copy live objects to to-space, swap halves"]
  SW --> R1["Fast, no moves, but fragments"]
  CO --> R2["No fragmentation, bump allocation, slowest pass"]
  CP --> R3["Cost scales with live data, needs 2x space"]
sections.caption: The three classic tracing strategies share a mark or trace step and differ in how they reclaim space, trading fragmentation, pause cost, and memory overhead.

sections.title: The Generational Hypothesis
sections.content:
Measurements across many languages show the **weak generational hypothesis**: **most objects die young**. Temporary strings, intermediate arrays from `map`/`filter`, request-scoped objects, closures for callbacks — the vast majority become garbage within moments of being allocated, while a small fraction (caches, application state, loaded modules) live for the whole program.

**Generational collectors** (David Ungar's "generation scavenging", 1984) exploit this by splitting the heap:

- The **young generation** (nursery) receives all new allocations. It is small and collected often by a **minor GC** — usually a copying collector, since cost is proportional to the few survivors.
- Objects that survive one or more minor GCs are **promoted** (tenured) into the **old generation**, which is large and collected rarely by a **major GC** (usually mark-sweep with occasional compaction).

The payoff is large: minor collections are cheap and short because they only touch live young objects, and the old generation is not scanned at all during them.

The complication is **old-to-young pointers**. To collect only the young generation, the GC must know about every old object that points into it — those references are effectively extra roots. Scanning the whole old generation would defeat the purpose, so runtimes track these pointers as they are created using a **write barrier** (a small piece of code the compiler emits on pointer stores) that records them in a **remembered set** or marks a **card table** entry ("this 512-byte card of old space contains a pointer into young space").

Practical consequences for you:

- **Short-lived allocation is cheap** in generational runtimes. Do not contort code to avoid small temporary objects.
- **Medium-lived objects are the expensive kind**: they survive long enough to be copied and promoted, then die in the old generation where reclamation is costlier. Caches with short TTLs and large per-request buffers kept across a few await points often fall here.
- **Premature promotion**: a burst of allocation can promote objects that would have died soon, bloating the old generation. Tuning young-generation size is a common GC knob for this reason.

sections.mermaid:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Nursery: new object allocated
  Nursery --> Reclaimed: dead at minor GC
  Nursery --> Intermediate: survives 1st scavenge
  Intermediate --> Reclaimed: dead at next minor GC
  Intermediate --> OldGen: survives 2nd scavenge, promoted
  OldGen --> OldGen: survives major GC
  OldGen --> Reclaimed: unreachable at major GC
  Reclaimed --> [*]
sections.caption: Object lifecycle in V8's generational heap. Most objects die in the nursery and are never copied; survivors of two scavenges are promoted to the old generation, which is collected rarely by the major mark-compact collector.

sections.title: Stop-the-World, Incremental, and Concurrent Collection
sections.content:
The simplest collector **stops the world (STW)**: it pauses every application thread (the **mutator**, in GC terminology), collects, then resumes. While paused, the object graph cannot change, so correctness is easy. The cost is **latency**: a 200 ms pause on a large heap means a dropped animation frame, a missed request deadline, or a timed-out health check.

Modern collectors reduce pauses with three techniques, often combined:

- **Parallel** — use multiple GC threads during the pause. Same pause model, shorter pause.
- **Incremental** — split the work into many small slices interleaved with the program (for example, 1 ms of marking every few milliseconds of JavaScript).
- **Concurrent** — run GC work on background threads *at the same time* as the program.

Incremental and concurrent marking introduce a hard problem: **the program keeps changing the graph while the collector is tracing it**. The standard model is **tri-color marking** (Dijkstra et al., 1978):

- **White** — not yet visited. Anything still white when marking finishes is garbage.
- **Grey** — visited, but its outgoing references have not been scanned yet (the worklist).
- **Black** — visited and fully scanned.

Marking finishes when no grey objects remain. The danger: if the program stores a reference to a **white** object into an already-**black** object *and* removes every other path to it from grey objects, the collector never revisits the black object and frees a live object. To prevent this, the compiler emits a **write barrier** on pointer stores:

- **Insertion (Dijkstra) barrier** — when a pointer to a white object is stored into a black object, shade the target grey. V8's marking barrier works this way.
- **Deletion / snapshot-at-the-beginning (Yuasa) barrier** — when a pointer is overwritten, shade the *old* target grey, so everything reachable at the start of marking survives. The JVM's G1 uses SATB.
- **Hybrid** — Go (since 1.8) combines both, which let it eliminate stack rescanning and cut pauses to sub-millisecond.

Moving collectors running concurrently also need **read barriers** or load barriers (ZGC, Shenandoah) so the program always sees an object's new address. Barriers cost a few percent of throughput — the price of short pauses. Every collector sits somewhere on the **throughput vs latency vs memory** triangle; you can usually pick two.

sections.mermaid:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> White: every object at mark start
  White --> Grey: reached from a root or a grey object
  Grey --> Black: all its references scanned
  White --> Grey: write barrier on black-to-white store
  Black --> [*]: survives, reset to white for next cycle
  White --> Freed: still white when no grey left
  Freed --> [*]
sections.caption: Tri-color marking. The marker turns grey objects black until none are grey; anything still white is freed. During concurrent marking, the write barrier shades a white object grey when the program stores it into a black object, so it cannot be lost.

sections.label: Tri-color marking & write barrier
sections.explanation: The marker scans root `A` (now black) and greys `B`, then pauses. The program moves the only reference to `C` from grey `B` into black `A`. Without a barrier, the marker never rescans `A`, `C` stays white, and it is swept even though `A` still points to it — a live object freed, the worst possible GC bug. With the Dijkstra insertion barrier, storing `C` into a black object shades it grey, so marking finds it and nothing live is swept.

sections.title: Inside V8: Orinoco, the Scavenger, and Concurrent Marking
sections.content:
V8 (Chrome, Node.js, Deno, Edge) has a generational heap and a collector project called **Orinoco**, whose goal is to move as much GC work as possible off the main thread.

**Young generation — the Scavenger.** New objects are bump-allocated in a small semi-space young generation. When it fills, a **minor GC (scavenge)** copies live objects into the other semi-space — a Cheney-style copying collector. The scavenger is **parallel**: several helper threads copy objects and update pointers simultaneously, so minor pauses are typically around a millisecond or less. Objects that survive **two** scavenges are **promoted** to the old generation. Old-to-young pointers are tracked by a write barrier and remembered sets, so a scavenge never scans old space.

**Old generation — the major mark-compact collector.**

- **Concurrent marking**: helper threads trace the old generation while JavaScript keeps running; the write barrier (an insertion-style marking barrier) keeps the tri-color invariant. Marking can also proceed incrementally on the main thread.
- A short **final atomic pause** finishes marking (rescanning roots, processing weak references).
- **Parallel compaction** of the most fragmented pages (evacuation) during the pause, and **concurrent sweeping** of the rest on background threads afterwards.

**Idle-time GC.** Chrome tells V8 when the main thread is idle (for example, between frames), and V8 schedules incremental GC work there so it does not compete with rendering.

What this means in Node.js and browsers:

- The old-generation limit is set by `--max-old-space-size=<MB>`. When a process nears it, V8 runs increasingly aggressive major GCs and finally crashes with *"FATAL ERROR: ... JavaScript heap out of memory"*. In containers, set it to fit the memory limit with headroom for buffers and native memory, which live outside the JS heap.
- `--trace-gc` prints one line per collection (type, heap sizes, pause time) — the quickest way to see whether GC is your latency problem.
- `node --expose-gc` exposes a global `gc()` for tests and demos only; calling it in production is almost always a mistake.
- `Buffer` and `ArrayBuffer` backing stores are allocated outside the V8 heap ("external memory"); their wrapper objects are tracked, so leaking the wrappers still leaks the memory.

sections.title: JVM and Go: Two Different Philosophies
sections.content:
**The JVM** offers several production collectors and lets you choose per workload (status as of JDK 25 LTS, September 2025):

- **G1 (Garbage-First)** — the **default** since JDK 9 on server-class machines. The heap is divided into equal-size regions, each acting as young or old; G1 collects the regions with the most garbage first and aims at a configurable pause target (`-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis`, default 200 ms). It uses concurrent marking with an SATB barrier and evacuates (copies) regions during pauses. A good balance of throughput and latency for most services.
- **ZGC** — a low-latency concurrent compacting collector using colored pointers and load barriers. Pause times are typically **well under a millisecond** and do not grow with heap size (heaps up to 16 TB). Generational ZGC arrived in JDK 21, became the default ZGC mode in JDK 23, and the non-generational mode was removed in JDK 24. Enable with `-XX:+UseZGC`.
- **Shenandoah** — Red Hat's concurrent compacting low-pause collector (`-XX:+UseShenandoahGC`); its generational mode became a product feature in JDK 25.
- **Parallel** (maximum throughput, longer pauses — batch jobs) and **Serial** (single-threaded; chosen automatically on very small machines or containers with under 2 CPUs or about 1.8 GB of memory, which surprises people running JVMs in tiny containers).

**Go** takes the opposite approach: **one collector, very few knobs**. It is a **concurrent, non-generational, non-moving tri-color mark-sweep** collector with a hybrid write barrier. Stop-the-world phases are short (typically well under a millisecond); most marking runs concurrently, using about 25% of available CPU while active, and goroutines that allocate heavily are drafted into "mark assist" to keep up. Because it does not move objects, Go relies on a size-class allocator (derived from TCMalloc) to limit fragmentation, and on **escape analysis** to keep many values on the stack so they never become garbage.

Go's two tuning knobs: **`GOGC`** (default 100 — start a cycle when the heap has grown 100% over the live heap after the last GC) and **`GOMEMLIMIT`** (since Go 1.19 — a soft total memory limit that makes the GC work harder as you approach it, essential in containers). Go 1.25 introduced the **"Green Tea"** collector as an experiment, which scans memory in page-sized batches for better cache locality, and Go 1.26 (February 2026) made it the default; the release notes expect roughly a 10–40% reduction in GC overhead for programs that lean heavily on the collector (opt out with `GOEXPERIMENT=nogreenteagc`, which is slated for removal in Go 1.27).

The contrast is instructive: the JVM optimises throughput and offers many trade-off points; Go optimises for low latency and simplicity, accepting more GC CPU and memory headroom in exchange.

sections.title: Rust: Ownership and Borrowing Instead of a Collector
sections.content:
Rust gets memory safety **without a garbage collector** by moving the "when can this be freed?" question to compile time.

1. **Ownership.** Every value has exactly one **owner** (a variable or a field). When the owner goes out of scope, the value is **dropped** — its destructor runs and its memory is freed, at a point the compiler knows statically. This is RAII made mandatory.
2. **Moves.** Assigning or passing a heap-owning value (`let b = a;` for a `String` or `Vec`) **moves** ownership; `a` becomes unusable, so there is never a second owner that could free it again (no double free).
3. **Borrowing.** Code can temporarily *borrow* a value without taking ownership: either **any number of shared references** (`&T`, read-only) **or exactly one mutable reference** (`&mut T`), never both at once. The **borrow checker** proves at compile time that no reference outlives the value it points to (no use-after-free, no dangling pointers) and that no data is mutated while aliased (no data races).

The result: deterministic, prompt freeing like C, safety like a GC'd language, and **no runtime collector, no pauses, and no heap headroom**. The costs are a steeper learning curve and patterns (graphs, doubly linked lists, observer webs) that fight single ownership.

For genuinely shared ownership, Rust provides **`Rc<T>`** (single-threaded reference counting) and **`Arc<T>`** (atomic, thread-safe), usually combined with `RefCell`/`Mutex` for mutation. Being reference counted, they leak on cycles; break cycles with **`Weak<T>`** back-pointers. Note that leaking is considered **memory-safe** in Rust — `std::mem::forget` and `Box::leak` are safe functions — because a leak cannot cause undefined behaviour, only waste.

Swift (ARC) and modern C++ (smart pointers plus RAII) sit in between: deterministic reference counting with programmer-managed weak references, but fewer compile-time guarantees than Rust's borrow checker.

sections.title: Weak References, Finalizers, WeakRef, and FinalizationRegistry
sections.content:
Sometimes you need to *refer to* an object without *keeping it alive*. That is what **weak references** are for. JavaScript offers three tools:

- **`WeakMap` / `WeakSet`** (ES2015) — keys are held weakly. When a key object becomes otherwise unreachable, its entry disappears. Keys must be objects (or non-registered symbols, since ES2023), and the collections are not iterable — you cannot observe which keys exist, which keeps GC timing unobservable. Ideal for attaching metadata to objects you do not own (DOM nodes, library objects) and for caches keyed by object identity.
- **`WeakRef`** (ES2021) — wraps a target; `ref.deref()` returns the object or `undefined` once collected. A target dereferenced during a synchronous job is kept alive until that job ends, so a freshly dereferenced object never vanishes mid-function.
- **`FinalizationRegistry`** (ES2021) — `registry.register(obj, heldValue)` asks for a callback with `heldValue` some time after `obj` is collected. Used to release *external* resources tied to JS objects (native handles, WebAssembly memory), and as a safety net, not a primary mechanism.

The specification is blunt about the limits: callbacks may run **late, in batches, or never** (for example, if the page closes or the registry itself is collected). Never put program logic in finalizers, never depend on them for closing files or connections, and remember that the held value must not reference the target (that would keep it alive). The TC39 proposal itself warns that correct use "takes careful thought, and they are best avoided if possible".

Other languages learned the same lesson. **Java's `finalize()`** was deprecated in JDK 9 and **deprecated for removal** in JDK 18 (JEP 421) because finalizers are slow, unpredictable, can resurrect objects, and may never run; use `try`-with-resources for deterministic cleanup and `java.lang.ref.Cleaner` as a fallback. C# pairs finalizers with `IDisposable` and `using`. Python's `__del__` runs promptly under refcounting but not reliably for cycles or at interpreter shutdown; use `with` blocks.

The general rule in every language: **use deterministic, explicit cleanup for resources** (`try/finally`, `with`, `using`, RAII; in JavaScript also the `using` declaration from the Explicit Resource Management proposal, already shipping in recent V8-based runtimes), and treat GC-triggered callbacks as best-effort hints.

sections.label: WeakRef & FinalizationRegistry
sections.explanation: `createPayload` makes a large object, records metadata in a `WeakMap`, registers it for finalization, and returns only a `WeakRef`, so no strong reference survives the call. The collection happens in a later macrotask because a target dereferenced in the current job is kept alive until the job ends. After `gc()`, `deref()` returns `undefined` and the `WeakMap` entry is gone with it. The finalizer then runs in a separate task — on current Node it reliably appears before `done`, but the spec allows engines to delay or skip it, so never depend on it. Run with `node --expose-gc`; `gc()` is for demos only.

sections.title: Common JavaScript Memory Leaks and How to Find Them
sections.content:
In a garbage-collected language a "leak" means **memory that is still reachable but no longer needed**. The usual suspects:

1. **Unbounded caches and maps** — module-level `Map`s, memoization caches, or arrays that only grow (per user, per URL, per request). Fix with size limits (LRU), TTLs, or `WeakMap` when keyed by objects.
2. **Forgotten event listeners and subscriptions** — `addEventListener`, `emitter.on`, RxJS/store subscriptions added on mount and never removed. In Node, a `MaxListenersExceededWarning` ("Possible EventEmitter memory leak detected") is a strong hint; raising the limit hides the leak. Fix with `removeEventListener`/`off`, an `AbortController` `signal`, or framework cleanup (React effect cleanup functions).
3. **Timers** — `setInterval` callbacks are roots until cleared, along with everything their closures capture.
4. **Closures retaining large data** — a long-lived callback that captures (or shares a scope with) a big array or response body.
5. **Detached DOM nodes** — elements removed from the document but still referenced from JavaScript (a cached element, a listener, a component instance), keeping the whole subtree alive.
6. **Accidental globals** — assigning to an undeclared variable in sloppy mode creates a global property (strict mode and modules turn this into an error).
7. **Retained logs** — objects passed to `console.log` stay alive while DevTools is open so you can inspect them.

**Finding leaks with heap snapshots.** A **heap snapshot** is a full dump of the JS heap: every object, its **shallow size** (its own bytes), its **retained size** (bytes freed if it were collected), and its **retainers** (who references it).

- **Browser**: DevTools → **Memory** → *Heap snapshot*. Filter by "Detached" to find detached DOM trees. *Allocations on timeline* shows which allocations survive.
- **Node**: start with `node --inspect` and open `chrome://inspect`, or write snapshots from code with `v8.writeHeapSnapshot()`, on a signal with `--heapsnapshot-signal=SIGUSR2`, or automatically near the limit with `--heapsnapshot-near-heap-limit=3`. Load the `.heapsnapshot` file in DevTools.
- **Technique (three snapshots)**: take a snapshot, perform the suspect action several times, take a second, repeat, take a third. In **Comparison** view, look for constructors whose count grows by a multiple of the repetitions. Pick one leaked object and read its **retainer chain** up to a root — the first link you did not expect (a `Map`, a listener array, a `(closure)` context) is the bug.

Before snapshots, confirm the leak: watch `process.memoryUsage().heapUsed` (or the browser's performance monitor) over time — a sawtooth that returns to the same baseline is healthy; a baseline that climbs after every major GC is a leak. Snapshots pause the process and can be as large as the heap, so be careful taking them in production.

sections.label: Leak and fix, measured
sections.explanation: `heapMB()` forces a full GC before reading `heapUsed`, so the numbers show *retained* memory rather than garbage waiting to be collected. The leaky handler stores every response in a module-level `Map` and adds a listener per request whose closure holds a 1,000-element array; after 5,000 requests about 42 MB is retained along with 5,000 listeners. The fixed version caps the cache at 100 entries (evicting the oldest via `Map` insertion order) and unsubscribes when each request ends, retaining almost nothing. Note `setMaxListeners(0)`: it silences Node's leak warning, which is exactly what you should *not* do in real code. Run with `node --expose-gc`; exact MB values vary by Node version.

sections.content:
**Common misconceptions**

- **"GC means no memory leaks."** GC frees *unreachable* memory. Reachable-but-useless data (caches, listeners, timers) leaks just as surely.
- **"Setting a variable to `null` frees the object."** It only removes one reference; the object is freed when *no* references remain and the collector runs.
- **"Cycles leak in JavaScript."** Not in any modern engine — tracing collectors handle cycles. They *do* leak under reference counting (Swift, `Rc`, `shared_ptr`, CPython without its cycle collector).
- **"Call `gc()` to fix memory problems."** Forcing collections cannot free reachable objects and usually hurts performance.
- **"Finalizers are destructors."** They may run late or never. Use `try/finally`, `with`, `using`, or RAII for resources.
- **"More heap is always better."** A larger heap means fewer collections but potentially longer major pauses and more memory cost; in containers, a heap limit above the container limit gets the process OOM-killed instead of a clean error.

items: **Manual** management (C `malloc`/`free`) is fast and predictable but invites leaks, use-after-free, and double frees — memory-safety bugs account for roughly 70% of serious vulnerabilities at Microsoft and Chromium. **Automatic** management (GC) trades CPU, pauses, and memory headroom for safety. **Ownership** (Rust, C++ RAII) frees deterministically at compile-time-known points.

Collectors treat **reachable as live**: anything reachable from **roots** (stack frames, registers, globals, runtime queues, registered listeners) survives. Reachable-but-unused data is the source of essentially all leaks in GC'd languages.

**Reference counting** frees objects the instant their count hits zero but cannot reclaim **cycles** and taxes every pointer write. CPython adds a generational cycle collector; **Swift ARC** has none, so you break cycles with `weak`/`unowned` (`[weak self]`). `shared_ptr` and Rust `Rc`/`Arc` need `weak_ptr`/`Weak` back-pointers.

**Tracing** algorithms: **mark-sweep** (no moving, fragments), **mark-compact** (no fragmentation, bump allocation, most expensive), **copying** (cost proportional to live data, needs 2x space). Real collectors combine them per generation.

The **generational hypothesis** — most objects die young — justifies a small, frequently copied **young generation** and a large, rarely collected **old generation**. Survivors are **promoted**; old-to-young pointers are tracked by a **write barrier** and a remembered set or card table.

**Stop-the-world** collection is simple but adds latency; **parallel**, **incremental**, and **concurrent** collectors shrink pauses. Concurrent marking uses **tri-color** (white/grey/black) marking and a **write barrier** (Dijkstra insertion, Yuasa/SATB deletion, or Go's hybrid) so a live object is never freed.

**V8 (Orinoco)**: a parallel copying **Scavenger** for the young generation (promotion after two survivals) and a mark-compact major GC with **concurrent marking**, parallel compaction, concurrent sweeping, and idle-time scheduling. Tune with `--max-old-space-size`; inspect with `--trace-gc`.

**JVM**: **G1** is the default (region-based, pause target); **ZGC** (generational-only since JDK 24) and **Shenandoah** give sub-millisecond-class pauses. **Go**: one concurrent, non-moving tri-color mark-sweep collector tuned by `GOGC` and `GOMEMLIMIT`, with the Green Tea collector as default since Go 1.26.

`WeakMap`/`WeakSet` hold keys weakly; `WeakRef` lets you observe an object without keeping it alive; `FinalizationRegistry` callbacks may run late or never. Never use finalizers (JS, Java's deprecated `finalize()`, Python `__del__`) for resource cleanup — use explicit `try/finally`, `with`, `using`, or RAII.

Common JS leaks: unbounded caches, forgotten listeners and subscriptions, uncleared intervals, closures over big data, detached DOM nodes, accidental globals. Find them by watching the post-GC baseline, then use the **three-snapshot** comparison in DevTools and follow the **retainer chain** of a leaked object to the root that holds it.

quiz.question: What does a tracing garbage collector consider "live"?
options: Objects that were accessed within the last GC cycle
Objects reachable through some chain of references from a root
Objects whose reference count is greater than zero
Objects created by the currently running function
quiz.explanation: Tracing GCs use reachability from roots (stack frames, registers, globals, runtime-held references) as the definition of live. Recent access is not tracked, and reference counts are what reference counting uses, not tracing.

quiz.question: Two objects reference each other and nothing else references either. Which strategy fails to reclaim them on its own?
options: Mark-sweep
Copying collection
Plain reference counting
Mark-compact
quiz.explanation: Each object keeps the other's count at 1, so reference counting never frees them. All tracing collectors start from roots, never reach the cycle, and reclaim it. That is why CPython adds a cycle collector and Swift requires weak references.

quiz.question: Why is a copying collector a good fit for the young generation?
options: Its cost is proportional to live objects, and most young objects are already dead
It never moves objects, so pointers stay valid
It needs no extra memory
It can only collect objects older than one cycle
quiz.explanation: A copying collector only touches survivors, and by the generational hypothesis few young objects survive. It does move objects (compacting them) and it needs a second space, which is affordable because the young generation is small.

quiz.question: In a generational collector, what is the write barrier's job with respect to old-to-young pointers?
options: It prevents old objects from ever pointing to young objects
It immediately promotes any young object referenced by an old one
It doubles the size of the young generation
It records the stores so a minor GC can treat those old-to-young references as roots without scanning the whole old generation
quiz.explanation: Minor GCs scan only the young generation, so references from old objects into it must be known. The barrier records them in a remembered set or card table, which the minor GC uses as extra roots.

quiz.question: During concurrent tri-color marking, the program stores a reference to a white object into a black object and deletes the only other path to it. What happens without a write barrier?
options: The collector detects the change at the next safepoint and rescans everything
The white object is freed even though it is still reachable
The black object is turned back to white automatically
Nothing; black objects are rescanned before sweeping
quiz.explanation: Black objects are not rescanned, and the white object is no longer reachable from any grey object, so it stays white and is swept while still referenced. Write barriers (Dijkstra insertion, Yuasa deletion, or hybrids) exist to prevent exactly this.

quiz.question: In V8, what happens to an object that survives two scavenges (minor GCs)?
options: It is promoted to the old generation
It is freed because it is considered stale
It is moved to a WeakMap
It is marked permanently and never collected
quiz.explanation: V8's Scavenger copies survivors between semi-spaces, and objects surviving a second scavenge are promoted to old space, where the major mark-compact collector handles them.

quiz.question: Which statement about current JVM garbage collectors is accurate?
options: ZGC is the default collector since JDK 21
The JVM has had only one collector since JDK 9
G1 is the default on server-class machines, and ZGC and Shenandoah are low-pause concurrent alternatives
Serial GC is never selected automatically
quiz.explanation: G1 has been the default since JDK 9. ZGC (generational-only since JDK 24) and Shenandoah are opt-in low-latency collectors. The JVM ships several collectors, and ergonomics picks Serial automatically on very small machines or containers.

quiz.question: How does Rust free heap memory without a garbage collector?
options: A background thread reference-counts every value
The programmer must call free() on every allocation
Memory is never freed until the process exits
Each value has one owner and is dropped when the owner goes out of scope, with the borrow checker ensuring no reference outlives it
quiz.explanation: Ownership plus compile-time borrow checking lets the compiler insert drops at known points. Reference counting exists only opt-in through Rc and Arc, and normal code never calls free manually.

quiz.question: Which use of FinalizationRegistry is appropriate?
options: Closing a database connection exactly when a wrapper object goes out of scope
As a best-effort safety net to release an external resource if the user forgot to call close()
Saving user data to disk when the page unloads
Counting how many objects are currently live for application logic
quiz.explanation: Finalization callbacks may run late, in batches, or never, so they cannot provide exact timing, guaranteed execution, or reliable counts. They are acceptable only as a backup to explicit cleanup such as close(), try/finally, or using.

quiz.question: You compare three heap snapshots taken around repeated "open and close modal" actions and see a growing number of detached HTMLDivElement objects. What should you look at next?
options: The retainer chain of one detached element, to find which reference keeps it reachable
The shallow size of the largest string in the heap
Whether --max-old-space-size is high enough
The number of times gc() was called
quiz.explanation: Detached elements that keep accumulating are still reachable from somewhere: a listener, a cached reference, or a component instance. The retainer chain shows the exact path from a GC root, which points to the code to fix. A larger heap limit only delays the crash.
